title: Wiggle Sort II
statement: Reorder the integer array `nums` in place so that its values go up and down in turn: `nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3] > ...`, with every comparison strict. The function returns nothing; the rearranged `nums` is the answer. The input is guaranteed to have at least one such ordering, and any ordering that follows the rule is accepted.
constraints: nums can always be reordered to follow the rule
notes:
## Intuition

A brute force could try orderings one by one, which is hopeless beyond tiny arrays. Instead, sort and split the values into a smaller half and a larger half: putting smaller values in the even slots and larger values in the odd slots gives every odd slot two smaller neighbours. The only danger is a value that sits on the split and has copies in both halves, such as the 5s in `[4, 5, 5, 6]`. Reading both halves from their high end puts the smaller half's copies of that value at the front of the even slots and the larger half's copies at the back of the odd slots, so they never meet whenever an answer exists. (The follow-up's O(n) version finds the median with quickselect and partitions around it, using the same placement.)

## Approach

1. Copy `nums` into `sorted` and sort it ascending.
2. The even slots need `ceil(n / 2)` values, so the smaller half is `sorted[0..small]` with `small = floor((n - 1) / 2)`; the larger half ends at `large = n - 1`.
3. Walk `i` over every slot. Even `i` takes `sorted[small]` and moves `small` down; odd `i` takes `sorted[large]` and moves `large` down.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 5, 1, 1, 6, 4]` sorts to `[1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 6]`, with `small = 2` and `large = 5`. Slot 0 gets `sorted[2] = 1`, slot 1 gets `sorted[5] = 6`, slot 2 gets `sorted[1] = 1`, slot 3 gets `sorted[4] = 5`, slot 4 gets `sorted[0] = 1` and slot 5 gets `sorted[3] = 4`, giving `[1, 6, 1, 5, 1, 4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the placement is one O(n) pass.
- Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

## Pitfalls

- Interleaving the halves from their low ends turns `[4, 5, 5, 6]` into `[4, 5, 5, 6]`, where `5 > 5` fails; take both halves from the top.
- With an odd length the smaller half gets the extra value, because there is one more even slot than odd slot.
- Read from the sorted copy, not from `nums`, or values are overwritten before they are placed.
- The answer is `nums` itself; returning a new array leaves `nums` unchanged.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sorted` | ascending copy of `nums` |
| `n` | number of values |
| `small` | next index of the smaller half to place, moving down |
| `large` | next index of the larger half to place, moving down |
| `i` | slot of `nums` being filled |

narration.2: Sort a copy so the smaller and larger halves are easy to pick from.
narration.3: Remember how many slots there are.
narration.4: The smaller half ends here; it has one extra value when n is odd.
narration.5: The larger half ends at the last index.
narration.6: Fill the slots from left to right.
narration.7: Even slots are the valleys of the wiggle.
narration.8: Place the largest value not yet used from the smaller half.
narration.9: Step down within the smaller half.
narration.11: Odd slots are the peaks: place the largest value not yet used from the larger half.
narration.12: Step down within the larger half.
